_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)
_sources.niddk: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones, read 2026-10-26: nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran listed among foods to reduce for calcium oxalate stones

vinegar.how: Use in dressings, marinades and quick pickles, or splash over cooked vegetables and beans.
vinegar.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
vinegar.reviewNote: The record is cider vinegar; other vinegars (balsamic, rice, wine) differ. A tablespoon supplies almost no nutrients. This profile makes no claim about blood sugar, weight or digestion.
vinegar.name: Vinegar

chocolate.how: Eat a small piece on its own, or chop into porridge, yoghurt and baking.
chocolate.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
chocolate.reviewNote: Dark chocolate 70–85% cacao; milk and white chocolate are different foods. Caffeine and theobromine are not in this nutrient set. Mineral content (iron, magnesium) comes with about 170 kcal and 12 g of fat per ounce.
chocolate.name: Chocolate

ketchup.how: Use as a condiment; a little goes a long way.
ketchup.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
ketchup.reviewNote: A condiment with added sugar and salt; a tablespoon supplies little of any nutrient. Sodium and added sugar are not shown in this nutrient set.
ketchup.name: Ketchup

turmeric.how: Add ground turmeric to curries, rice, soups and roasted vegetables; it stains, and a little black pepper is a common pairing in cooking.
turmeric.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
turmeric.reviewNote: Ground turmeric as a spice. Per 100 g it has very high iron (55 mg), but a teaspoon is 3 g, so it adds about 1.7 mg at most. Curcumin content is not in this record, and this profile makes no claim about turmeric supplements or inflammation.
turmeric.name: Turmeric

spirulina.how: Stir a small amount into smoothies, juices or dressings; it has a strong, earthy taste.
spirulina.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
spirulina.reviewNote: Dried spirulina. Quality, contamination and vitamin B12 forms differ between products and are not covered by this record (USDA lists B12 as 0).
spirulina.name: Spirulina

avocado-oil.how: Use for roasting, sautéing and dressings.
avocado-oil.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
avocado-oil.reviewNote: A pure oil: about 14 g of fat and 124 kcal per tablespoon with no meaningful vitamins or minerals in the USDA record.
avocado-oil.name: Avocado oil

coconut-oil.how: Use for sautéing and baking where a coconut flavour is welcome.
coconut-oil.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
coconut-oil.reviewNote: A pure oil, mostly saturated fat; no meaningful vitamins or minerals. The record is coconut oil (not hydrogenated). This profile makes no health claim about coconut oil.
coconut-oil.name: Coconut oil

olive-oil.how: Use for sautéing, roasting and dressing salads and vegetables.
olive-oil.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
olive-oil.reviewNote: The USDA record is olive oil for salad or cooking; extra-virgin oil may have other compounds that are not in this nutrient set.
olive-oil.name: Olive oil

honey.how: Stir into tea, yoghurt or porridge, or use in dressings and marinades.
honey.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
honey.reviewNote: Honey is mostly sugar: about 17 g of carbohydrate and 64 kcal per tablespoon with trace minerals.
honey.name: Honey

maple-syrup.how: Drizzle over porridge and yoghurt, or use in baking and dressings.
maple-syrup.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
maple-syrup.reviewNote: Pure maple syrup, not pancake-syrup blends. Mostly sugar: about 13 g of carbohydrate and 52 kcal per tablespoon.
maple-syrup.name: Maple syrup

tamari.how: Use in stir-fries, marinades and dipping sauces; start with a small amount since it is salty.
tamari.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tamari.reviewNote: Tamari is very high in sodium (not shown in this nutrient set); the USDA record is a generic tamari. Tamari is often sold as wheat-free but labels vary, so people avoiding gluten should check the label.
tamari.name: Tamari
